exam: A 55‑year‑old HIV patient presents with dyspnea; echo shows EF 30 % – what is the first drug to start? — ACE inhibitor to improve survival and remodeling.
A patient with EF 38 % develops atrial fibrillation – what anticoagulation strategy is appropriate? — Start warfarin or DOAC if renal function allows, given EF <40 %.
A 60‑year‑old man with EF 25 % has sudden chest pain – what is the priority investigation? — Immediate ECG and troponin to rule out acute MI.
A patient with EF 45 % has worsening edema despite diuretics – what is the next step? — Add a beta‑blocker and reassess volume status.
A 50‑year‑old woman with EF 32 % is on NSAIDs for arthritis – what is the risk? — NSAIDs can worsen renal function and fluid retention, increasing mortality.
A patient with EF 28 % is stable on ACEI and beta‑blocker but has persistent fatigue – what additional therapy may help? — Consider adding a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist.
ai.title: Left Ventricular Ejection Fraction
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: LVEF is the percentage of blood the left ventricle ejects each beat. It predicts prognosis in heart failure, guides therapy, and flags severe systolic dysfunction.

sections.p: LVEF is calculated from ventricular volumes: EF = (EDV‑ESV)/EDV ×100. It is measured by echocardiography, cardiac MRI, or radionuclide ventriculography. In low‑resource settings, a basic M-mode or 2‑D echo is often used.

t.b: What is the systolic function? A reduced EF indicates impaired contractility; normal EF suggests preserved systolic function.
What is the most accurate EF? MRI gives the gold standard EF, useful when echo is suboptimal.
What is the EF when echo is unavailable? Provides reliable EF in patients with poor acoustic windows.

sections.p: The ESC and ACC guidelines classify systolic heart failure by EF: HFrEF (<40 %), HFmrEF (40–49 %), HFpEF (≥50 %). In practice, <35 % is considered high‑risk and warrants aggressive therapy.

In East Africa, the leading causes of reduced EF are ischemic heart disease, rheumatic heart disease, HIV‑associated cardiomyopathy, and malaria‑related myocarditis. Other contributors include hypertension, anemia, and herbal cardiotoxins.

Patients with low EF often have exertional dyspnea, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, fatigue, and peripheral edema. In acute decompensation, they may present with pulmonary oedema or cardiogenic shock.
Start with a focused history, exam, ECG, chest X‑ray, and basic labs. If available, echo is mandatory. When echo is not available, consider bedside ultrasound or clinical scoring.

t.b: What is the rhythm and ischemic changes? ST‑segment changes or arrhythmias suggest ischemia or myocarditis.
What is the cardiac silhouette? Enlarged LV or pulmonary congestion indicates heart failure.
What is renal function and electrolytes? Hyperkalaemia or renal failure influence drug choice.
What is the EF? Provides immediate systolic function assessment when formal echo is unavailable.

sections.p: Severe low EF (<35 %) is associated with arrhythmias, thromboembolism, sudden cardiac death, and cardiogenic shock. Watch for hypotension, syncope, and worsening dyspnea.
Treat the underlying cause first. In HFrEF, start ACE inhibitor or ARB, beta‑blocker, and diuretic. Avoid NSAIDs and nephrotoxic drugs. Consider anticoagulation if EF <35 % with atrial fibrillation.

sections.p: Re‑evaluate EF every 6–12 months or sooner if symptoms change. Counsel on salt restriction, fluid balance, smoking cessation, and vaccination against influenza and pneumococcus.
Reduced EF can mimic pulmonary hypertension or restrictive cardiomyopathy. Distinguish by imaging (LV dilation vs. normal size) and by clinical context.
In severe anemia or hyperthyroidism, EF may appear normal despite poor contractility. A low EF can be falsely normal in early ischemia if echo windows are poor.
